# How to Ask Alexa+ to Read Recipe Steps Out Loud While You Cook

> **In short:** Alexa+ can read a recipe one step at a time, pause when you ask, and resume where you left off — so your phone stays out of the messy work zone. You need an Echo or another Alexa device, a free Amazon account, and the recipe text handy. Some recipe features require Alexa+, Amazon's newer assistant, so older Alexa devices may show the older experience.

Picture the moment your hands are covered in bread dough and the next instruction says "fold in the chocolate chips." You'd rather not fumble for the phone, wipe flour across the screen, and risk losing your spot three lines down. Alexa+ — Amazon's upgraded assistant — is designed for exactly this kind of moment. Once you set it up, you speak naturally and it reads the next step out loud, waits for your voice to say "next," and picks up exactly where you stopped. This guide shows you how to set that up and walk through a real recipe hands-free.

## Before you start

- You already use Alexa on an Echo, Echo Dot, Echo Show, or another Alexa-enabled device, and your Amazon account is linked to it (assume this is set up — we don't redo it here).
- **Plan check**: Amazon says Alexa+ is available to a growing set of users, including through Amazon Prime; access can vary by device and region. If your device shows the older Alexa experience, some steps below may not appear — the fallback notes tell you what to do.
- The recipe text — a URL, a paragraph you copied, or something in your own words. A few specific sites work best, but plain text works too.
- A quiet kitchen background helps, but Alexa+ is built to handle typical kitchen noise.
- **Total time**: about 10 minutes for the first setup; after that, 30 seconds per recipe.

## Step 1 — Open the Alexa app and check that Alexa+ is active

Open the **Alexa app** on your phone, tap the **Devices** tab at the bottom (look for a speaker or smart-home icon if your app layout differs), and choose the Echo you're going to cook with. On the device page, look for any banner, badge, or label that mentions **Alexa+**. If you see it, you're on the upgraded experience and the recipe flow below should be available. If your app instead shows the standard Alexa screens, the recipe flow may be limited or absent — Amazon has been rolling Alexa+ out gradually, so this is normal.

💬 Example: ask yourself, "Do I see a label that says Alexa+ on this device's page?"

You'll know it worked when you can confirm whether your device is on Alexa+ or the older Alexa, so you know which features to expect in the next steps.

## Step 2 — Pick a recipe source Alexa+ understands well

Recipes work best when Alexa+ has clean, structured text to read. The most reliable options are: a public recipe webpage URL (the kind you'd send to a friend), the text of a recipe pasted into a note or message, or describing the recipe in plain words yourself ("a simple chocolate chip cookie recipe"). Open your phone, find the recipe, and either copy the URL or copy the full ingredient + step list into a single text block. Avoid screenshots and PDF scans — Alexa+ reads text, not images.

💬 Example: copy this URL style — `example.com/recipes/chocolate-chip-cookies` — into your clipboard, or paste the steps you want to follow into a single note.

You'll know it worked when you have either a URL on your clipboard or a clean text block ready, and your phone is somewhere dry and safe.

## Step 3 — Wake Alexa+ and hand it the recipe

Stand within normal voice range of your Echo (a few feet, not across the room), say the wake word — "Alexa" — and follow it with a single sentence that gives Alexa+ the recipe and tells it how to behave. The simplest phrase that usually works is: *"Alexa, read this recipe: [paste or say the recipe text]."* If you have the URL on your clipboard, try: *"Alexa, walk me through this recipe"* and then read the URL aloud once. Alexa+ will usually repeat the recipe back, summarize the ingredients, and ask if you want to start. Tap nothing — just answer by voice.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, walk me through a chocolate chip cookie recipe. One cup of butter, one cup of sugar, two cups of flour, one teaspoon baking soda, half a teaspoon salt, two cups chocolate chips. Bake at 350 for 12 minutes."*

You'll know it worked when Alexa+ reads back the ingredients in order and asks, in some form, whether you're ready to start cooking.

## Step 4 — Cook along step by step using only your voice

Say *"start"* or *"begin"* (or the phrase Alexa+ just offered you). It will read step one out loud. When you finish that step, say **"next"** to hear step two. If you're mid-step and need to wash your hands or chop something, say **"pause"** or **"wait"**; say **"resume"** to pick back up. If a step was unclear, say **"repeat that"** or **"say that again"** and Alexa+ will re-read the same step. If you ever lose track, say **"what step am I on?"** and Alexa+ will tell you. You can also jump around with **"go back one step"** or **"skip to the last step"** for things like total cook time.

💬 Example: while kneading dough, simply say, *"Alexa, next"* — no phone, no tapping, no flour on a screen.

You'll know it worked when you can move from ingredient to plated dish without ever touching your phone, and Alexa+ never loses your place even after long pauses.

## Step 5 — Set a cooking timer without breaking your flow

Hands covered in oil? Say **"Alexa, set a timer for 12 minutes"** without leaving the recipe. Alexa+ runs timers in the background and chimes when time is up; it does not interrupt the recipe audio unless you ask. You can name timers so you remember which is which: *"Alexa, set a pasta timer for 9 minutes"* versus *"Alexa, set a sauce timer for 4 minutes."* To cancel, just say **"cancel the pasta timer"** by name. This works whether or not a recipe is currently being read.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, set an oven timer for 12 minutes."* Then, when it rings, *"Alexa, next."*

You'll know it worked when the timer chimes over the recipe audio and your phone stays exactly where you put it.

## Step 6 — Convert measurements on the fly when a recipe is in metric

Many online recipes use grams and milliliters. While a step is being read, ask **"how much is 200 grams of flour in cups?"** and Alexa+ will answer in US cups and ounces, then return to the recipe when you say **"continue."* You can also ask the reverse: *"how many tablespoons in a quarter cup?"* for spoon-based shortcuts. This is one of the most useful moments in a recipe, because it's the exact instant you'd normally need to scrub your hands.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, how many cups is 200 grams of butter?"* then *"continue."*

You'll know it worked when you hear a clear conversion in US measurements and the recipe picks up at the same step you were on.

## Step 7 — Wrap up, save what worked, and bookmark the recipe

When the final step is read, Alexa+ usually says something like "enjoy your meal" or asks if you'd like a summary. You can ask **"Alexa, save this recipe"** to keep it for next time in the Alexa app, or **"Alexa, send this recipe to my phone"** to receive a text version you can re-open later. If neither option is offered on your device, take 30 seconds now to screenshot or copy the recipe text into a note titled with the dish name — that's your personal cookbook. Wipe down your Echo's top edge if it got splashed; that area is the only part that needs drying.

💬 Example: *"Alexa, send this recipe to my phone"* — then check the Alexa app's **Activity** or **Notifications** section for the message.

You'll know it worked when you can find the recipe again next week without searching, and your phone never had to leave the counter.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting the recipe from the Alexa home screen instead of via a clear command.** If you just say "Alexa," it opens the generic assistant. Lead with intent: *"Alexa, walk me through this recipe"* — that triggers the cooking flow.
- **Reading a URL too fast or skipping ahead.** Speak the link slowly and as one chunk. If Alexa+ misheard it, say **"try the next result"** or **"use the second link"** rather than repeating the whole URL.
- **Assuming Alexa+ always knows what's on your screen.** It doesn't see your phone. If you want it to use a recipe on a webpage, you have to either paste the text or read the URL aloud — pasting silently won't transfer.
- **Letting timers pile up.** Three timers chiming at once is worse than none. Cancel by name as you go: *"cancel the sauce timer."*

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** On weeknights, the recipe-on-the-counter, phone-on-the-couch setup becomes normal again. You'll cook more often because the friction of cleaning your hands between steps is gone — and you'll stop losing your place at step four of seven.
- **For your business or work:** If you teach cooking, host supper clubs, or run a food-related small business, you can rehearse recipes aloud, time multiple dishes in parallel without a stopwatch, and record the recipe text for handouts — all from one Echo.
- **If you want to go further:** Try the same hands-free flow with a multi-step workflow that isn't a recipe — a workout routine, a kid's bedtime checklist, or a DIY repair. The voice commands — *next, pause, repeat, resume, what step am I on* — transfer directly, and Alexa+ will treat any numbered list you give it like a recipe.

## Try it now

Pick one recipe you already know by heart — say, scrambled eggs or your morning coffee — and say out loud right now: *"Alexa, walk me through making scrambled eggs. Three eggs, butter, salt, pepper, low heat, stir constantly, serve when just set."* Then cook it using only your voice. You'll feel in the first two minutes why this is worth setting up before the next messy recipe.
